edges.description: Localized disruption of airway branching morphogenesis produces the defining hamartomatous cystic pulmonary lesion.
Cystic dilatation of disorganized terminal airway structures forms the characteristic pulmonary cysts.
Malformed cystic pulmonary airway structures carry an ongoing risk of local morbidity including recurrent pulmonary infections.
Rupture or air-trapping of malformed cystic airway spaces leads to pneumothorax.
Clonal KRAS-mutant mucinous cell clusters within type 1 CPAM epithelium act as precursors that can progress to well-differentiated mucinous adenocarcinoma.
edges.source: Somatic KRAS Mutations and Mucinous Cell Clusters

edges.description: Large space-occupying CPAM lesions (high CPAM volume ratio) compress intrathoracic structures and lead to fetal hydrops.
Mass effect of a large lesion on adjacent lung and mediastinum produces neonatal respiratory distress.
Severe macrocystic CPAM mass effect and cardiac compression manifest clinically as fetal hydrops (ascites and fetal scalp edema).
Impaired drainage and disorganized airways within the malformed lobe predispose to recurrent localized pulmonary infection.
Air-trapping and rupture of subpleural cystic spaces can produce spontaneous pneumothorax.

nodes.description: Anatomic lobectomy is the most common definitive surgical treatment for CPAM in U.S. pediatric practice, used in approximately 88% of resections, and is increasingly performed via video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS), which is associated with shorter hospital stay and lower 30-day complication rates than open lobectomy.

evidence.reference_title: Lobectomy vs. sublobar resection for congenital pulmonary airway malformations: a 10-year NSQIP-pediatric review.
evidence.snippet: VATS was utilized more often than open surgery for both lobectomy (57.8%) and sublobar resections (54.7%) and was associated with lower 30-day complication rates (OR 0.58, p < 0.01) and total hospital length of stay (-1.48 days, p < 0.0001) after lobectomy.

nodes.description: CPAM arises from a localized disruption of airway branching morphogenesis during fetal lung development, producing a hamartomatous overgrowth of terminal bronchiolar/airway structures with cystic dilatation. The presumed level of the tracheobronchial tree at which the developmental insult occurs underlies the Stocker subtype histology, and mixed type-1/type-2 patterns support a continuum model.
